title: Customers with a High-Value Transaction
statement: First name, last name and Account ID of customers who have ever made a transaction of strictly greater than 30000. Use aliases as “First_Name”, “Last_Name” and “Account_ID”.
solution:
SELECT DISTINCT c.FirstName AS First_Name,
       c.LastName  AS Last_Name,
       c.AccountID AS Account_ID
FROM Customers c
JOIN Transactions t ON c.AccountID = t.AccountID
WHERE t.TransactionAmount > 30000;
explain: Join the two tables on AccountID, keep transactions above 30000 (strictly, so exactly 30000 is excluded), and use DISTINCT so a customer with several big transactions appears only once.

topic: GROUP BY + COUNT + SUM + ORDER BY
title: Department Salary Summary
statement: The department name (use alias 'DeptName'), the count of doctors (use alias 'TotalDoctors'), and the total salary (use alias 'TotalSalary') for each department. Sort the results by the total salary in descending order.
solution:
SELECT DeptName,
       COUNT(*)    AS TotalDoctors,
       SUM(Salary) AS TotalSalary
FROM Doctors
GROUP BY DeptName
ORDER BY TotalSalary DESC;
explain: GROUP BY DeptName makes one row per department; COUNT(*) counts its doctors and SUM(Salary) adds their salaries. ORDER BY TotalSalary DESC puts the highest total first.

title: Students in Room R1
statement: The student ID, first name, last name of students enrolled in a course held in room 'R1'. Use aliases “Student ID”, “First Name”, “Last Name”. Show each student only once.

cols.name: Room
cols.desc: Room in which the course is held

solution:
SELECT DISTINCT s.StudentID AS "Student ID",
       s.FirstName AS "First Name",
       s.LastName  AS "Last Name"
FROM Students s
JOIN Courses c ON s.StudentID = c.StudentID
WHERE c.Room = 'R1';
explain: Aliases containing a space must be quoted ("Student ID" or `Student ID`). Join on StudentID and filter Room = 'R1' exactly; LIKE 'R1%' would wrongly include room R10. DISTINCT removes a student who has two courses in R1.

title: Above Department Average
statement: The name (alias 'Employee_Name'), department ID (alias 'Dept_ID') and salary (alias 'Salary') of every employee who earns more than the average salary of their own department.
solution:
SELECT e.EmpName AS Employee_Name,
       e.DeptID  AS Dept_ID,
       e.Salary  AS Salary
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.Salary > (SELECT AVG(x.Salary)
                  FROM Employees x
                  WHERE x.DeptID = e.DeptID);
explain: The inner query is correlated: it runs for each outer row and averages only that employee's department (x.DeptID = e.DeptID). Comparing with the company-wide average is the common mistake.

title: Products Never Ordered
statement: The name (alias 'Product_Name') and price (alias 'Price') of products that have never been ordered.
solution:
SELECT p.ProductName AS Product_Name,
       p.Price       AS Price
FROM Products p
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON p.ProductID = o.ProductID
WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL;
explain: A LEFT JOIN keeps every product; products with no matching order get NULLs in the Orders columns, so WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL keeps exactly those. NOT IN (SELECT ProductID FROM Orders) or NOT EXISTS also work.

title: Second Highest Salary
statement: The second highest distinct salary in the Staff table, with alias 'Second_Highest'. If several people share the highest salary, the second highest is the next lower amount.

cols.name: StaffID
cols.desc: Unique ID of the staff member

explain: The subquery finds the top salary; the outer MAX takes the largest salary below it. This handles ties at the top, while ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 would return the top salary again. SELECT DISTINCT Salary ... ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 is another correct way.

title: Order Count per Customer
statement: Every customer's name (alias 'Customer_Name') and the number of orders they placed (alias 'Total_Orders'). Customers with no orders must appear with 0. Sort by Total_Orders in descending order, then by Customer_Name in ascending order.
solution:
SELECT c.CustomerName    AS Customer_Name,
       COUNT(o.OrderID)  AS Total_Orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY Total_Orders DESC, Customer_Name ASC;
explain: LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders. COUNT(o.OrderID) counts only real orders, so it gives 0 for them; COUNT(*) would count the NULL-filled row and give 1. An INNER JOIN would drop them.

title: Departments with More Than Two Employees
statement: The department (alias 'Department') and its number of employees (alias 'Employee_Count') for departments that have more than 2 employees. Sort by Department in ascending order.
solution:
SELECT Department,
       COUNT(*) AS Employee_Count
FROM Employees
GROUP BY Department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY Department;
explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use COUNT; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. "More than 2" means > 2, so a department with exactly 2 employees is excluded.

title: Employee and Manager Names
statement: Each employee's name (alias 'Employee') with their manager's name (alias 'Manager'). Employees without a manager must still appear, with Manager as NULL. Sort by Employee in ascending order.

cols.name: ManagerID
cols.desc: EmpID of the employee's manager (NULL for the top manager)

solution:
SELECT e.EmpName AS Employee,
       m.EmpName AS Manager
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.ManagerID = m.EmpID
ORDER BY Employee;
explain: A self join uses the same table twice with different aliases: e for the employee, m for the manager. LEFT JOIN keeps employees whose ManagerID is NULL.

title: Top 3 Scorers
statement: The name (alias 'Player_Name') and score (alias 'Score') of the 3 players with the highest scores, highest first.
solution:
SELECT PlayerName AS Player_Name,
       Score
FROM Players
ORDER BY Score DESC
LIMIT 3;
explain: Sort by Score descending and keep the first 3 rows with LIMIT 3 (SQL Server uses SELECT TOP 3, Oracle uses FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY).

title: Filter Customers by Name, City and Age
statement: The name (alias 'Name'), city (alias 'City') and age (alias 'Age') of customers whose name starts with 'A', who live in Pune or Delhi, and whose age is between 25 and 40 (both included). Sort by Name in ascending order.
solution:
SELECT Name, City, Age
FROM Customers
WHERE Name LIKE 'A%'
  AND City IN ('Pune', 'Delhi')
  AND Age BETWEEN 25 AND 40
ORDER BY Name;
explain: 'A%' means starts with A (% = any characters; '%A%' would match an A anywhere). IN checks a list of values, and BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends.

title: Total Marks and Grade
statement: Each student's name (alias 'Student_Name'), total marks in the three subjects (alias 'Total') and grade (alias 'Grade'): 'A' if Total is 240 or more, 'B' if Total is 180 or more, otherwise 'C'. Sort by Total in descending order.
solution:
SELECT StudentName AS Student_Name,
       Maths + Science + English AS Total,
       CASE
           WHEN Maths + Science + English >= 240 THEN 'A'
           WHEN Maths + Science + English >= 180 THEN 'B'
           ELSE 'C'
       END AS Grade
FROM Results
ORDER BY Total DESC;
explain: Columns can be added in SELECT. CASE checks conditions top to bottom and returns the first match, so the >= 240 test must come before >= 180. 'or more' means >=.

title: Premium Book Categories
statement: For each category whose average book price is greater than 400, show the category (alias 'Category'), the number of books (alias 'Book_Count') and the average price rounded to 2 decimal places (alias 'Avg_Price'). Sort by Avg_Price in descending order.
solution:
SELECT Category,
       COUNT(*)             AS Book_Count,
       ROUND(AVG(Price), 2) AS Avg_Price
FROM Books
GROUP BY Category
HAVING AVG(Price) > 400
ORDER BY Avg_Price DESC;
explain: Group by Category, keep groups with HAVING AVG(Price) > 400 (an average of exactly 400 is excluded) and round only for display with ROUND(AVG(Price), 2).

title: Duplicate Email Addresses
statement: Every email address that is used by more than one user (alias 'Email') and how many times it appears (alias 'Occurrences'). Sort by Email in ascending order.
solution:
SELECT Email,
       COUNT(*) AS Occurrences
FROM Users
GROUP BY Email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY Email;
explain: Grouping by Email puts identical addresses together; HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only those that repeat. This is the standard way to find duplicate values.

title: Highest Paid Employee in Each Department
statement: For each department, the employee(s) with the highest salary in that department: department (alias 'Department'), name (alias 'Employee_Name') and salary (alias 'Salary'). If two people tie for the top salary, show both. Sort by Department, then by Employee_Name.
solution:
SELECT e.Department,
       e.EmpName AS Employee_Name,
       e.Salary
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.Salary = (SELECT MAX(x.Salary)
                  FROM Employees x
                  WHERE x.Department = e.Department)
ORDER BY e.Department, Employee_Name;
explain: The correlated subquery finds each department's maximum, and the outer query keeps every employee earning exactly that, so ties are kept. Selecting EmpName with GROUP BY Department is not valid standard SQL (MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY rejects it) and can only return one name per group.
